featured.alt: Open vintage manuscript with Arabic script on a dark background.
featured.caption: An open manuscript in Arabic script: the written record, and not only the message, is what taḥrīf concerns.

inline.alt: Section of the Great Isaiah Scroll, a Hebrew manuscript from the Dead Sea caves.
inline.caption: The Great Isaiah Scroll, one of the oldest surviving manuscripts of a biblical book, found near the Dead Sea.

inline.alt: Close-up of an open Bible showing printed Old Testament text.
inline.caption: A printed Bible: Muslim scholars asked which of its words come from revelation and which from later hands.

inline.alt: Folio from a Quran in early Kufic script, 8th to 9th century.
inline.caption: A Quran folio in Kufic script, 8th to 9th century: the book that Muslims hold as the criterion over the earlier scriptures.

featured.alt: Interior of an ornate mosque dome with complex geometric patterns.
featured.caption: A mosque dome of geometric pattern, an art that points to God without picturing Him.

inline.alt: Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, in Arabic calligraphy on aged paper.
inline.caption: Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) in calligraphy: the verse that speaks of God's knowledge and throne.

inline.alt: Milky Way over a desert mountain at night.
inline.caption: The night sky over a desert: the Quran points to creation as a sign of the Creator, who is not like it (42:11).

inline.alt: Persian mosque dome ceiling with turquoise geometric pattern.
inline.caption: A tiled dome with a pattern that repeats without a centre, an image of the infinite and not of God.

featured.alt: Masjid al-Nabawi in Medina at night with lit minarets.
featured.caption: Medina at night: the city where the early community debated the ruling on mutah, temporary marriage.

inline.alt: Illustrated Arabic manuscript page with calligraphy and floral ornament.
inline.caption: An illustrated Arabic manuscript page. The rulings on mutah were recorded and argued over in books of hadith and law.

inline.alt: Camel riders crossing red desert dunes under a cloudy sky.
inline.caption: Travellers crossing the desert. The short permission for mutah came on campaigns and journeys, far from home.

inline.alt: Minarets at sunset in Konya, Türkiye.
inline.caption: Minarets at sunset in Konya. Sunni and Shia scholars still differ on whether mutah remains lawful.

featured.alt: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina on a clear day.
featured.caption: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina, the mosque of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, where Muslims send blessings upon him and worship God alone.

inline.alt: Worshippers praying in rows at a mosque in Jakarta, Indonesia.
inline.caption: Muslims pray in straight rows, and the prayer is addressed to God alone.

inline.alt: Arabic calligraphy in gold on a stone wall.
inline.caption: Gold calligraphy of the kind that carries the testimony of faith: Muhammad is the servant and messenger of God.

inline.alt: Mosque courtyard with tall minarets and a blue sky.
inline.caption: A mosque courtyard. The call to prayer from its minarets names God first and then the Prophet's mission.

featured.alt: Dome of Istiqlal Mosque in Jakarta, Indonesia.
featured.caption: Istiqlal Mosque in Jakarta, in Indonesia, a country with one of the largest Muslim populations in the world.

inline.alt: Thousands of pilgrims around the Kaaba in Mecca.
inline.caption: Pilgrims at the Kaaba in Mecca. Muslims are one of the most widely spread faith communities.

inline.alt: World map showing the continents.
inline.caption: A world map. Pew Research Center's count of Muslims by country covers the decade from 2010 to 2020.

inline.alt: Busy market in Amman, Jordan, with traditional goods.
inline.caption: A market in Amman, Jordan: a Muslim-majority country in the Middle East and North Africa region.

featured.alt: Hira Cave on Jabal al-Nour near Mecca under a blue sky.
featured.caption: Jabal al-Nour near Mecca, with the cave of Hira where the first revelation came to Muhammad ﷺ.

inline.alt: Open Quran with a green cover lit by sunlight.
inline.caption: An open Quran. Its challenge to produce a chapter like it (2:23) is part of how Muslims answer the charge.

inline.alt: The Kaaba at dusk in Mecca with a clear sky.
inline.caption: The Kaaba at dusk in Mecca, the city where Muhammad ﷺ was born and first called people to God.

inline.alt: Visitors climbing the rocky slope of Jabal al-Nour near Mecca.
inline.caption: Visitors climbing Jabal al-Nour, the mountain above the cave of Hira, near Mecca.

featured.alt: Al-Azhar Mosque in Cairo with domes and minarets.
featured.caption: Al-Azhar in Cairo, founded in 970 and among the oldest universities still teaching.

inline.alt: Collection of old manuscripts in Arabic script.
inline.caption: Arabic manuscripts. Scholars of the Islamic world preserved, translated and added to the sciences of earlier peoples.

inline.alt: Close-up of an antique globe showing constellations.
inline.caption: An antique celestial globe. Astronomers in the Islamic world refined the star tables and instruments of antiquity.

inline.alt: Turquoise dome and tiles of a madrasa in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
inline.caption: A madrasa in Samarkand, where Ulugh Beg founded a madrasa and an observatory in the 15th century.
